new_statements.quote: The most prominent syllable in a word receives primary stress. For the placement of primary stress a few generalizations hold. These are not without exceptions. There are various cases where the position of primary stress is not in line with the generalizations. The location of primary stress is therefore partly a lexical property of words. [...] The main generalization as to the location of primary stress in native words is that it usually is on the only or the first (left-most) full vowel, which is also the case in Dutch. The non-native part of the Frisian lexicon consists of loanwords, which enter Frisian via Dutch. In general, then, the stress pattern of loan words is the same as that of their Dutch counterparts.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Two strata. Native words contain one full vowel (the rest schwa) and stress falls on that only/first full vowel, so native simplex words are effectively initial-stressed (Sipma 1913 sec. 87: 'Simple words.. have the stress on the first syllable'). Loanwords, which enter via Dutch, keep the Dutch pattern: stress within the last three syllables, never on schwa, directly before a schwa syllable, not on the antepenult when the penult is closed, and final when the last syllable is superheavy (long vowel+C, diphthong+C, V+CC); these are tendencies with lexical exceptions (kanon 'cannon' vs kanon 'canon').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Visser & Weening 'Secondary stress' topic: secondary stress is largely predictable from main stress by alternation (Alternating Stress Principle, supplemented by the Hammock Principle), only in words of three or more syllables, e.g. ˌre.sul.'taat 'result', ˌle.di.'kant 'bedstead'; it has the same phonetic correlates (amplitude, duration, pitch) to a lesser degree. Sipma 1913 sec. 86 distinguishes stressed, half-stressed and unstressed syllables, with half-stress on certain suffixes (-dom, -heit, -skip, -achtich, -loas, -lei).
new_statements.exceptions: 'These are not without exceptions.. The location of primary stress is therefore partly a lexical property of words'; loanword generalizations 'present (more or less strong) tendencies'; superheavy-final counterexamples leraar, bamboes, arbeid, ambacht, maarskalk; Sipma: initial stress 'does not always apply to words of foreign origin', prefixes bi-/ge-/for-/ont-/to- unstressed, compounds have no simple rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (lexical stress of simplex and complex words); Taalportaal keeps word stress distinct from sentence accent ('a stressed syllable is louder, longer, and is spoken on a slightly higher pitch'; duration the strongest cue, citing Rietveld & van Heuven 1997). Standard West Frisian as described by the Fryske Akademy phonologist; the authors note 'there is not much literature on Frisian stress' and that the Frisian and Dutch systems 'match to a great extent'.
new_statements.identity_note: west2863 is not a language: Glottolog 5.3 lists it under Bookkeeping ('This entry has been retired and is featured here only for bookkeeping purposes'; 'Retired in ISO 639-3: Change to [fry] to align with ISO 639-2', effective 2005-11-16, no references). The variety it once denoted is Modern West Frisian = ISO fry = glottocode west2354 (Fryslân, Netherlands), which is ALREADY in the catalog (record 'Modern West Frisian', classification weight-hedged, Sipma 1913 secs. 84-92 + Visser & Weening 2015 Taalportaal; check status 'well-sourced'). by our rule that each source is filed under the language's current Glottolog code (a retired code does not make a separate language) this key must not become a second entity; fold it into west2354.

sources.note: Native words: primary stress on the only or first (left-most) full vowel (native words have one full vowel, other syllables schwa); loanwords keep the Dutch pattern; the generalizations have exceptions so stress location is partly lexical; correlates amplitude, duration, pitch, duration strongest.

sources.note: Loanwords follow the Dutch system (Kager 1989, Booij 1995): three-syllable window, no stress on schwa, stress directly before a schwa syllable, closed-penult restriction; tendencies, not exceptionless. This is the page the existing west2354 catalog record cites.

sources.note: Secondary stress predictable from main stress by alternation (Alternating Stress Principle + Hammock Principle); only in words of 3+ syllables; e.g. ˌre.sul.'taat, ˌle.di.'kant; authors note there is little literature on Frisian stress and the topics are modelled on the Dutch ones.

sources.note: Final superheavy syllables (long vowel+C, diphthong+C, short vowel+CC) strongly attract final primary stress in polysyllables (akút, klimaat, fontein, orkest), with a few counterexamples (leraar, arbeid, ambacht).

sources.note: Chapter 'Stress' secs. 84-93, pp. 19-20: simple (non-compound, non-derivative) words stressed on the first syllable, not always in foreign words; three degrees of stress; prefixes bi-/ge-/for-/ont-/to- unstressed (stress on stem), ant-/oar-/on- stressed in nouns; some suffixes full-stressed (-inne, -aezje, -ier, -ij, -eare) or half-stressed; compounds have no simple rule; level stress in some compounds.
